author: goldturtle
body:
@marcfeuermann @pgaudet: submitted with the PAINT issue template's fields. The posting account cannot set labels, so please add `PAINT annotation` (and `high priority`, if you agree).

* **PTHR ID & PTN node:** PTHR11256; PTN000135648 (family root; gain of positive regulation of apoptotic process, GO:0043065); PTN000135647 (v1 gain of negative regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway, GO:2001243; dropped)

* **Sequences with problematic annotation (ID + gene/protein name):** UniProtKB:P10415 BCL2 (BCL2 apoptosis regulator); UniProtKB:Q07817 BCL2L1 (BCL2 like 1); UniProtKB:Q92843 BCL2L2 (BCL2 like 2); UniProtKB:Q9HD36 BCL2L10 (BCL2 like 10); UniProtKB:Q16548 BCL2A1 (BCL2 related protein A1)

* **Type of Issue:** Erroneous propagation: the root gain reaches the anti-apoptotic members. Several of its source annotations are also erroneous (see the note on the evidence for the root gain). BCL2L10 may act both ways and may need its own decision.

*How this draft was made:* an automated screen compared every PAN-GO (IBA) annotation of human genes (release 2025-10-12_2.0.5, PANTHER 19) with the genes' experimental annotations in GO release 2025-10-10. Flagged annotations were then judged by evidence-cited reasoning (Claude subagents, citing only a curated evidence pack). The statements below were checked against the GO, PAN-GO and PANTHER data, and the papers behind the key annotations were read. Please treat it as a candidate for curator review.


**Related tracker issue:** [geneontology/go-annotation#5449](https://github.com/geneontology/go-annotation/issues/5449) (2024): apoptosis terms (extrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in absence of ligand, intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to DNA damage, release of cytochrome c from mitochondria) were blocked for the fly anti-apoptotic members Buffy and Debcl at the same root node, PTN000135648.

In the current model, *positive regulation of apoptotic process* ([GO:0043065](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0043065)) is gained at the family root and inherited by the anti-apoptotic members, including BCL2. The earlier gain of *negative regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway* ([GO:2001243](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:2001243)) on the anti-apoptotic branch is gone. BCL2 now has an IBA to positive regulation of apoptosis and none to negative regulation, the opposite of its experimental annotations.

**Inherited:** BCL2 `involved_in` *positive regulation of apoptotic process* ([GO:0043065](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0043065))

- **Gain:** PTN000135648 (duplication, Eumetazoa; the family root, with all 9 human paralogs below), dated 2025-09-02.
- **Evidence genes (16):** 8 from the pro-apoptotic BAX, BAK1 and BOK (human, mouse, rat); 6 from anti-apoptotic members (*C. elegans* ced-9, human MCL1, mouse Mcl1, Bcl2l1 and Bcl2l10, rat Bcl2l1); 2 zebrafish genes, baxb in the BAX clade (listed in the tree as zgc:112983) and bcl2l16 in the BCL2L10 clade. BCL2 itself is not among them.
- **Losses of this term in the family:** PTN000135883 (zebrafish BOK duplicates) and PTN002600738 (protostome BOK clade), both IRD, 2025-09-02. There is none on the anti-apoptotic branch.
- **Human genes inheriting it:** BCL2, BCL2L1, BCL2L2, BCL2L10 and BCL2A1 (anti-apoptotic); BAK1 and BOK (pro-apoptotic). BAX and MCL1 inherit the more specific *positive regulation of neuron apoptotic process* instead (BAX from PTN008515428, MCL1 from PTN002600668). PAN-GO leaves out an inherited term when a more specific one is inherited. MCL1's gain rests only on annotations of human MCL1 and mouse Mcl1 to *positive regulation of oxidative stress-induced neuron intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway* ([GO:1903378](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:1903378); [PMID:23858059](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23858059/)) that reverse their paper, which shows Mcl-1 as the prosurvival factor; the same paper gives Prkn the negative-regulation term.
- **v1 (paper release):** the term was gained at PTN000883418 (Deuterostomia; dated 2020-10-23; evidence: BAX from human, mouse, rat and zebrafish) and inherited by BAX only.

**Dropped since v1:** *negative regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway* ([GO:2001243](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:2001243)), gained at PTN000135647 (dated 2017-02-28; evidence: human BCL2 and BCL2L1, zebrafish bcl2l1 (formerly bcl2l), mouse Bcl2l10). In v1 it was inherited by BCL2, BCL2L1, BCL2L2, BCL2L10 and MCL1, so the v1 tree (PANTHER 15) placed all five under this node. In the current tree PTN000135647 (speciation, Bilateria; CED-9 subfamily) covers only BCL2, BCL2L1 and BCL2L2. It carries no annotation, and no node on BCL2's path below the root carries any.

**BCL2's own experimental annotations** (GO release 2025-10-10) against *positive regulation of apoptotic process*: 20 opposing, 0 supporting. They include *negative regulation of apoptotic process* ([GO:0043066](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0043066)) from 15 papers, e.g. [PMID:21212266](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21212266/), [PMID:9027314](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9027314/) and [PMID:7650367](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7650367/). BCL2's only annotations to [GO:0043065](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0043065) are the IBA and one NAS ([PMID:14634621](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14634621/)), a ComplexPortal annotation of the BAD:BCL2 complex that reflects BAD's action.

**Literature (Textpresso, all species corpora):** 55 sentences mention BCL2 together with *apoptotic process*. By cue words, 20 describe the opposite of the inherited direction and 10 agree.

> Other dysfunctions The expression of mutant forms of BAG3 (p.R128W and p.L462P) in rat neonatal cardiomyocytes (RNC) induces an increase in sensitivity to apoptosis due to serum depletion (Table 1). **BAG-3 binds the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2, enhancing the anti-apoptotic effect of BCL2 in cells of various tumors 56–58.** This function has yet to be confirmed in vivo because of the lack of a specific animal model of BAG3-related MFM.

— Batonnet-Pichon S, Behin A, Cabet E, Delort F, Vicart P, Lilienbaum A (2017). Myofibrillar Myopathies: New Perspectives from Animal Models to Potential Therapeutic Approaches. *Journal of neuromuscular diseases*. [PMID:28269794](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28269794/).


> This interpretation was further supported by genetic evidence. **We crossed Rad50 S/S with Eµ-Bcl2 mice, which carry a transgene of the anti-apoptotic BCL2 gene (Strasser et al. 1990).** This transgene increases resistance to apoptosis in B and T lymphocytes (Strasser et al. 1991a,b).

— Morales M, Theunissen JW, Kim CF, Kitagawa R, Kastan MB, Petrini JH (2005). The Rad50S allele promotes ATM-dependent DNA damage responses and suppresses ATM deficiency: implications for the Mre11 complex as a DNA damage sensor. *Genes & development*. [PMID:16357220](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16357220/).


**Sentences counted as agreeing** (10): none of them describes BCL2 itself promoting apoptosis. They are about pro-apoptotic relatives (BAX, BAK, BH3-only proteins) or the family as a whole, and several call BCL2 anti-apoptotic in the same sentence. Two examples:

> **PAK1 enhances beta cell survival by inactivating the pro-apoptotic factor BCL2-associated agonist of cell death (BAD) and activating the anti-apoptotic BCL2 apoptosis regulator (BCL2).**

— Ahn M, Dhawan S, McCown EM, Garcia PA, Bhattacharya S, Stein R et al. (2025). Beta cell-specific PAK1 enrichment ameliorates diet-induced glucose intolerance in mice by promoting insulin biogenesis and minimising beta cell apoptosis. *Diabetologia*. [PMID:39404845](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39404845/).


> **BCL2 proteins control mitochondrial dynamics in apoptotic cells In mammals, overexpression of the proapoptotic BCL2 family member Bax promotes Drp1-dependent mitochondrial fragmentation.**

— Rolland SG, Conradt B (2010). New role of the BCL2 family of proteins in the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics. *Current opinion in cell biology*. [PMID:20729050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20729050/).


Reviews: Reed et al. 1998, [PMID:9714773](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9714773/), [doi:10.1016/s0005-2728(98)00108-x](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0005-2728(98)00108-x); Tsujimoto & Shimizu 2000, [PMID:10648802](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10648802/), [doi:10.1016/s0014-5793(99)01761-5](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0014-5793(99)01761-5).

**Note on the evidence for the root gain:** six of the 16 evidence genes are anti-apoptotic, and most of their annotations do not show the protein promoting apoptosis:

- *C. elegans* ced-9 (EXP, [PMID:10846174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10846174/)) and human MCL1 (IDA, [PMID:21132008](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21132008/)) are ComplexPortal annotations of complexes (CED-9:EGL-1 and CED-9:CED-4; MCL1:NOXA). The papers show CED-9 and MCL1 as the inhibitors.
- Human MCL1 (IGI) and mouse Mcl1 (IMP) from [PMID:23858059](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23858059/) reverse their paper (see above).
- Rat Bcl2l1 (IMP, [PMID:22158476](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22158476/)) comes from a paper whose experiments target Bim (Bcl2l11), not Bcl-xL: probably the wrong gene.
- Mouse Bcl2l1 (IDA, [PMID:8798158](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8798158/)) is for the pro-apoptotic isoform Bcl-xS (GAF column 17: PR:Q64373-2).
- Only mouse Bcl2l10 (Diva, IDA, [PMID:9829980](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9829980/)) and zebrafish bcl2l16 (Bcl-wav, IDA, [PMID:24778760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24778760/)) are pro-apoptotic results for the main protein, both in the BCL2L10 branch. Another paper on mouse Bcl2l10 ("Boo", [PMID:9878060](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9878060/)) reports it as anti-apoptotic.

**Reasoning** (evidence-cited; verdict *error likely*, high confidence; cause: paralog inheritance): BCL2 inherits 'positive regulation of apoptotic process' from the root duplication node of the BCL2 family, whose evidence genes include the pro-apoptotic effectors BAX, BAK1 and BOK. About 19 independent papers (IDA/IMP/IGI) annotate BCL2 to the opposite term, and the literature consistently calls it anti-apoptotic. The term was probably passed to BCL2 from paralogs with the opposite function, and a loss is missing on BCL2's lineage.

- *Against:* BCL2 has 20 experimental annotations from about 19 separate papers, all to negative regulation of apoptosis or its subtypes, mostly IDA, IMP or IGI. ([PMID:1373874](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1373874/); [PMID:7546744](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7546744/); [PMID:8358790](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8358790/); [PMID:17289999](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17289999/); [PMID:28280358](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28280358/); [PMID:15006356](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15006356/); [PMID:20097879](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20097879/); [PMID:11684014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11684014/))
- *Against:* The term was gained at a Eumetazoa duplication node. Its evidence genes include BAX, BAK1 and BOK, which GO-CAM shows acting as channels in intrinsic apoptotic signaling, the opposite role to BCL2's. (PANTHER tree; BAX; BAK1; BOK; gomodel:69b3372b00001963; gomodel:62b4ffe300003618)
- *Against:* Literature sentences call BCL2 anti-apoptotic and say it blocks apoptotic death. One sentence suggests anti-apoptotic family members arose by duplication and loss of an ancestral killing function, which is exactly the situation where a root-level gain needs losses on the anti-apoptotic lineages. (Batonnet-Pichon et al. 2017; Morales et al. 2005; Bargiela et al. 2015; Strasser and Vaux 2018)
- *Context:* Reviews describe the BCL-2 family as containing opposing pro-survival and pro-apoptotic members. (Kaloni et al. 2023; Youle and Strasser 2008; Rubin et al. 2000)
- *For:* Some evidence genes closer to BCL2, the ortholog ced-9 and the paralog Bcl2l1, support the inherited term, possibly from context-specific findings. The pack contains no pro-apoptotic evidence for BCL2 itself. (ced-9; Bcl2l1)
- *Context:* The term was absent from BCL2 in v1, and the existing losses are at nodes with no human genes. (PAN-GO v1; PAN-GO loss)

*Reasoner's suggested fix:* Add a loss (NOT) of [GO:0043065](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0043065) on BCL2's anti-apoptotic lineage: at least at PTN002600681, or at PTN000135647 after checking ced-9's positive-regulation evidence. Restore an IBA for negative regulation of (intrinsic) apoptotic process on that lineage. *Tree check:* A loss at PTN000135647 would cover evidence genes (Bcl2l1 (MOUSE), Bcl2l1 (RAT), ced-9 (CAEEL)), contradicting them. A loss at PTN000135647 also removes the term from BCL2L1, BCL2L2.

*Note on the reasoning:* No single node groups the anti-apoptotic members: MCL1 and BCL2A1 share a branch with BAX, and the CED-9 subfamily node PTN000135647 holds evidence genes (see the suggested change below). The ced-9 annotation behind the 'for' claim comes from ComplexPortal annotations of two CED-9 complexes (with EGL-1 and with CED-4), whose paper shows CED-9 as the inhibitor (see the note on the root gain).

**The other anti-apoptotic members** inherit the same annotation. The literature screen flagged BCL2, BCL2L1 and BCL2L10. Reasoning verdicts: BCL2L1: *error likely* (medium confidence); BCL2L2: *error likely* (medium confidence); BCL2L10: *acceptable, the gene acts both ways* (medium confidence); BCL2A1: not among the strong findings.

**Suggested change:**

- Restore a negative-regulation gain ([GO:2001243](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:2001243), or [GO:0043066](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0043066)) at PTN000135647.
- For *positive regulation of apoptotic process*, no single loss can cover the anti-apoptotic members. They sit in three of the root's five branches: PTN000883460 (BCL2, BCL2L1, BCL2L2), PTN008515446 (BCL2L10) and PTN000883411 (MCL1 and BCL2A1, a branch shared with BAX). Evidence genes for the term also sit among them: ced-9 and rat and mouse Bcl2l1 under PTN000135647, mouse Bcl2l10 under PTN000135812, zebrafish bcl2l16 in the BCL2L10 branch, and human MCL1 and mouse Mcl1 in the MCL1 branch.
- The cleaner fix is to move the gain from the root to the three pro-apoptotic clades, which hold all of their own evidence genes: BAX at PTN008515428 (below the branch it shares with MCL1 and BCL2A1), BAK1 at PTN008318549 and BOK at PTN000883439. Most anti-apoptotic evidence annotations do not hold up (see the note on the root gain), so this loses little. The exception is the BCL2L10 branch (mouse Diva, zebrafish Bcl-wav), which may need its own decision, as BCL2L10 may act both ways.
- Correct the source annotations listed in the note on the root gain (ComplexPortal, ParkinsonsUK-UCL and RGD), and MCL1's inherited *positive regulation of neuron apoptotic process* will lose its only basis.
- If losses are preferred instead, three sit directly below paralog evidence genes: BCL2 at PTN002600681 (Euteleostomi), BCL2L2 at PTN008964526 (Tetrapoda) and BCL2A1 at PTN002600722 (Euteleostomi). For BCL2 and BCL2L2, *C. elegans* ced-9, a distant ortholog, is an evidence gene further up (under PTN000135647). The evidence annotations under PTN000135647 do not show the main proteins promoting apoptosis: ced-9's and rat Bcl2l1's look mis-curated, and mouse Bcl2l1's is correct but only for the Bcl-xS isoform. So a single loss at PTN000135647 (BCL2, BCL2L1, BCL2L2) is defensible if the first two are corrected and the isoform annotation is not taken to speak for the gene. For BCL2L1 and BCL2L10 the only subclades without evidence genes are primate-only (PTN000135702 and PTN000135813, Catarrhini), directly below their own rodent orthologs, which are evidence genes (mouse and rat Bcl2l1; mouse Bcl2l10). That is a conflict with orthologs, so review those annotations rather than add a loss.
- *Release of cytochrome c from mitochondria* ([GO:0001836](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0001836)) is also gained at the root (dated 2023-11-28), and BCL2 inhibits this process. Three of its sources are anti-apoptotic. Two reverse their paper: the IDAs of human BCL2L1 and mouse Bcl2 ([PMID:9843949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9843949/)) come from a study in which Bcl-xL and Bcl-2 *inhibited* Bax-induced mitochondrial changes, so they should be *negative regulation of release of cytochrome c from mitochondria* ([GO:0090201](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0090201)). BCL2's own NAS ([PMID:9027314](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9027314/)) and ISS ([PMID:9843949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9843949/)) to [GO:0001836](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0001836) have the same problem. The third, mouse Bcl2l1 (IGI with Bax, acts upstream of or within; [PMID:17052454](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17052454/)), comes from a study of a BAD BH3 peptide that binds Bcl-xL; it could not be checked in full text and may be worth reviewing too.

### References
- Ahn M, Dhawan S, McCown EM, Garcia PA, Bhattacharya S, Stein R et al. (2025). Beta cell-specific PAK1 enrichment ameliorates diet-induced glucose intolerance in mice by promoting insulin biogenesis and minimising beta cell apoptosis. *Diabetologia*. [PMID:39404845](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39404845/).
- Bargiela A, Cerro-Herreros E, Fernandez-Costa JM, Vilchez JJ, Llamusi B, Artero R (2015). Increased autophagy and apoptosis contribute to muscle atrophy in a myotonic dystrophy type 1 Drosophila model. *Disease models & mechanisms*. [PMID:26092529](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26092529/).
- Batonnet-Pichon S, Behin A, Cabet E, Delort F, Vicart P, Lilienbaum A (2017). Myofibrillar Myopathies: New Perspectives from Animal Models to Potential Therapeutic Approaches. *Journal of neuromuscular diseases*. [PMID:28269794](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28269794/).
- Kaloni D, Diepstraten ST, Strasser A, Kelly GL (2023). BCL-2 protein family: attractive targets for cancer therapy. *Apoptosis*. [PMID:36342579](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36342579/).
- Morales M, Theunissen JW, Kim CF, Kitagawa R, Kastan MB, Petrini JH (2005). The Rad50S allele promotes ATM-dependent DNA damage responses and suppresses ATM deficiency: implications for the Mre11 complex as a DNA damage sensor. *Genes & development*. [PMID:16357220](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16357220/).
- Reed JC, Jurgensmeier JM, Matsuyama S (1998). Bcl-2 family proteins and mitochondria. *Biochim Biophys Acta*. [PMID:9714773](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9714773/).
- Rolland SG, Conradt B (2010). New role of the BCL2 family of proteins in the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics. *Current opinion in cell biology*. [PMID:20729050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20729050/).
- Rubin GM, Yandell MD, Wortman JR, Gabor Miklos GL, Nelson CR, Hariharan IK et al. (2000). Comparative genomics of the eukaryotes. *Science (New York, N.Y.)*. [PMID:10731134](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10731134/).
- Strasser A, Vaux DL (2018). Viewing BCL2 and cell death control from an evolutionary perspective. *Cell death and differentiation*. [PMID:29099481](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29099481/).
- Tsujimoto Y, Shimizu S (2000). Bcl-2 family: life-or-death switch. *FEBS Lett*. [PMID:10648802](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10648802/).
- Youle RJ, Strasser A (2008). The BCL-2 protein family: opposing activities that mediate cell death. *Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol*. [PMID:18097445](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18097445/).
title: PAINT issue: PTHR11256 (BCL-2 family): root gain of "positive regulation of apoptotic process" is inherited by the anti-apoptotic BCL2, BCL2L1, BCL2L2, BCL2L10 and BCL2A1

author: goldturtle
body: Update after checking the latest annotation data (UniProt-GOA human file of 2026-11-04): the gain of *positive regulation of apoptotic process* (GO:0043065) at PTN000135648 now has a 17th evidence gene, zebrafish baxa (ZFIN:ZDB-GENE-000511-6), which is pro-apoptotic. This does not change the case. The other inherited annotations named in this issue, the dropped GO:2001243 gain, BCL2's own experimental annotations and the human source annotations cited above are unchanged.
